cereal-or-granola-bar-kelloggs-special-k.title: Cereal or granola bar (Kellogg's Special K bar)

content.title: About
content.content: Kellogg's Special K Bar is a crunchy granola‑style snack bar enriched with whole grains, dried fruit and a light yogurt coating. It is marketed as a quick on‑the‑go snack that provides sustained energy and a feeling of fullness between meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The Special K Bar was first launched in the early 2000s as part of the Special K line aimed at health‑conscious consumers.
The bar contains whole wheat, oat and rice grains together with dried fruits such as cranberries and raisins.
In some markets the bar is finished with a thin yogurt glaze that adds a creamy flavor.
It is positioned as a "low‑calorie" snack and often featured in weight‑management campaigns.
Packaging is made from recyclable plastic in line with the brand's sustainability initiatives.

items.title: Source of whole grains
items.content: Whole grains provide complex carbohydrates that release energy slowly, helping to maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and contributes to a feeling of satiety.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The bar contains a small amount of fat, mostly unsaturated, making it suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: B‑vitamin content
items.content: Includes vitamins B1, B2 and B6, which are involved in energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron helps maintain normal blood formation and oxygen transport.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The bar contains wheat and oats, so it is not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Added sugars
items.content: Despite being low‑calorie, the product contains added sugars, which may be a concern for diabetics.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: The combination of complex carbs and sugars can raise blood glucose quickly in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Nut and dried‑fruit allergens
items.content: Some variants include nuts or dried fruits that can trigger allergic reactions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The bar is convenient to carry as a snack between meals, at the gym, or while traveling. It can be broken into pieces and added to yogurt, oatmeal or a smoothie for extra texture and flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the package tightly sealed to prevent moisture absorption and loss of crunch.

content.title: About
content.content: Pork roll is a piece of pork meat, usually from the loin or shoulder, formed into a roll shape and often filled with spices, herbs, vegetables, or cheese. After shaping, the roll is baked or roasted, resulting in a juicy, flavorful product that can be sliced into convenient portions.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pork roll is a common festive dish in Russia and Eastern European countries.
Traditional fillings may include garlic, paprika, mustard, and sauerkraut.
In some regions the roll is made with dried fruits such as apricots or raisins for a sweet‑savory contrast.
Pork is a good source of vitamin B12 and iron, especially when using lean cuts.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Pork provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains vitamins B1, B3, B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc is important for immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Heme iron
items.content: Iron from pork is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Selenium content
items.content: Selenium has antioxidant properties and supports thyroid health.

items.title: High in saturated fat
items.content: Excessive consumption may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked roll can harbor pathogens such as Salmonella or Campylobacter.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pork proteins.

items.title: Sodium in marinades
items.content: Pre‑marinated rolls often contain a lot of salt, which is undesirable for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pork roll can be served hot as a main dish, sliced thin for sandwiches, added to salads, or used as an appetizer. It pairs well with mustard, barbecue sauce, sauerkraut, and mashed potatoes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked roll in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Scones are small British baked goods that resemble a dense, dry biscuit. They are traditionally made from flour, butter, milk or buttermilk, a leavening agent, and a modest amount of sugar. Scones are often served with jam, clotted cream, or butter, especially alongside tea.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Scones originated in Scotland in the 19th century and quickly spread throughout the United Kingdom.
The word “scone” comes from the Scottish “scone,” likely related to the Old English “scōn,” meaning a piece of bread.
The classic serving method is “cream tea,” which pairs scones with clotted cream and jam.
There are many variations: with raisins, blueberries, cheese, ham, or even savory herbs.
In the United States scones are often sweeter and glazed, whereas British scones are usually less sweet.

items.title: Source of whole grains
items.content: When made with whole‑grain flour, scones provide dietary fiber, B‑vitamins, and minerals.

items.title: Contains calcium
items.content: Using buttermilk or milk in the dough adds calcium, which supports bone health.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: The carbohydrates in scones are readily digestible, making them a convenient pre‑activity snack.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Additions such as dried fruit, nuts, or berries can supply iron, potassium, and vitamin C.

items.title: High sugar and fat content
items.content: Traditional scones contain generous amounts of butter and sugar, increasing their calorie density.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Standard flour contains gluten, so scones are unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Recipes often include dairy, eggs, and sometimes nuts, which are common allergens.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Scones are best served warm, split in half, and spread with butter, jam, or clotted cream. They can be enjoyed as a snack, part of breakfast, or used as a base for savory sandwiches with ham and cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep scones in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze them in bags and reheat in the oven before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Split pea soup with meat is a classic Russian dish made from dried peas, meat (usually beef or pork), vegetables, and spices. The soup is thick, hearty, and carries the distinctive earthy flavor of peas combined with the richness of meat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pea soup has been a staple in Russian cuisine since medieval times.
Traditional recipes often include smoked ham or bacon, giving the broth a subtle smoky aroma.
In some regions the soup is finished with sautéed carrots or a spoonful of sauerkraut for extra tang.
Even after long cooking, peas retain a high proportion of their nutrients.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Peas provide about 25 % protein, making the soup a good protein source, especially if the meat is reduced or replaced with plant alternatives.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of iron and zinc
items.content: Meat contributes easily absorbed iron and zinc, essential for immune function and energy production.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Peas have a low GI, which helps maintain stable glucose levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The soup supplies B1, B6, and folate, supporting nervous system health and metabolism.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Using ready‑made broth or adding excessive salt can make the soup too salty.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Peas can cause gas in sensitive stomachs; soaking them before cooking reduces this effect.

content.title: How to Serve
content.content: Serve the soup hot, often with a slice of rye bread or croutons. Garnish with fresh parsley or dill and a dollop of sour cream if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze for up to 2 months; thaw in the fridge and reheat gently on the stove.

tea-iced-brewed-black-decaffeinated-unsw.title: Tea, iced, brewed, black, decaffeinated, unsweetened

content.title: About
content.content: Iced, brewed, black, decaffeinated, unsweetened tea is a refreshing beverage made from black tea leaves that are first brewed and then chilled. The caffeine is removed and no sugar is added, making it low‑calorie and suitable for those avoiding stimulants and sweeteners.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black tea is the world’s second most consumed beverage after water.
Cold‑brew retains many of the antioxidants found in hot‑brew tea.
Decaffeination is usually done by water or CO₂ processes, preserving leaf flavor.
Without sugar, the tea has a naturally slightly bitter taste that becomes more pronounced when chilled.
In some cultures, iced black tea is served with a slice of lemon or mint for extra aroma.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Black tea contains polyphenols that help combat free radicals and support cellular health.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Regular tea consumption may help lower cholesterol levels and improve vessel function.

items.title: Improves hydration
items.content: Unsweetened iced tea is a tasty way to increase fluid intake, especially in warm weather.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: The absence of sugar and caffeine makes this drink virtually calorie‑free, useful for weight management.

items.title: Stress reduction
items.content: L‑theanine in tea can promote relaxation without causing drowsiness.

items.title: Tea allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to tea components.

items.title: Iron absorption
items.content: Tannins can reduce iron absorption from meals, so it’s best not to drink tea with main meals.

items.title: Fluoride content
items.content: Excessive consumption may lead to fluoride buildup, which can affect dental health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the iced tea on its own, or add a slice of lemon, mint leaves, or berries for extra flavor. It also works well as a base for non‑alcoholic cocktails.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared beverage in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑5 days. Discard if it becomes cloudy, develops an off‑smell, or changes taste.
